parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man books an eye test at an optician's.
script: Hello. I'd like to book an eye test, please.
Of course. Have you been to us before?
No, this is my first time.
Then I'll need some details. What's your name?
Leon Fisher. F, I, S, H, E, R.
The twelfth of April, nineteen ninety-eight.
Is there any particular reason for the test?
I've been finding it hard to read road signs when I'm driving, especially at night.
When did you last have your eyes tested?
Do you wear glasses or contact lenses at the moment?
We have an appointment on Tuesday at four forty-five p.m. Would that suit you?
Are you a student, by any chance? Tests are free for full-time students.
Yes, I'm doing a master's degree.
Then the test will be free. Please bring your current prescription if you have it.
And one more thing. We may use eye drops during the test, so please don't drive afterwards. Your vision may be blurred for a few hours.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A guide shows visitors around a historic sailing ship.
script: Welcome aboard the Morning Star. My name's Hugh, and I'll be your guide today.
The Morning Star was launched in 1890. She was a fast sailing ship, built to carry tea from China to Britain, and she competed with other ships to deliver the new season's tea first.
After many years of neglect, she was badly damaged in a storm in 1998, and the restoration you see today took more than ten years.
You're free to explore all the decks, but for safety reasons, visitors are not allowed to climb the rigging.
Let me explain what you'll find on each part of the ship. On the upper deck, you can try the interactive steering wheel and see what it was like to steer through a storm.
At the stern, at the back of the ship, you'll find the captain's cabin, with its original furniture.
On the middle deck, you can see where the sailors slept, in hammocks hung close together.
Down in the lower hold, we've recreated the cargo, with hundreds of wooden tea chests.
Underneath the ship, in the dry dock, there's a collection of figureheads, the carved figures that decorated the front of ships.
And finally, in the galley, which was the ship's kitchen, you can see the stove where the cook prepared meals for thirty men.

groups.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

items.q: When was the Morning Star launched?
What was the ship's main purpose?
What are visitors not allowed to do?

groups.instr: What can visitors see in each part of the ship? Choose SIX answers from the list, A–G.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two tourism students, Isla and Dev, evaluate a city's tourism website.
script: Isla, let's go through our evaluation of the city tourism website.
OK. Overall, I think the biggest weakness is that it's very hard to navigate on a phone. The menus don't fit on the screen.
Agreed, and most tourists use phones. On the positive side, the photos are excellent. They really make you want to visit.
Yes. But I was surprised that there's no information at all for disabled visitors, for example about wheelchair access.
That's a serious omission. And for our user testing, we asked ten international students to complete tasks on the site, like finding a hotel.
Right. Let's rate each section. The homepage is excellent. It's attractive and clear.
But the events calendar is poor. Half the events listed had already happened.
The accommodation search is adequate. It works, but there aren't many filters.
The maps are poor. They don't show public transport at all.
And the language options are adequate. There are five languages, but some translations are clearly automatic.

groups.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

items.q: What is the biggest weakness of the website?
options: It is hard to use on phones.

items.q: What do they like about the website?
How did they test the website?
options: by asking students to complete tasks

items.q: How many people tested the website?

groups.instr: How do they rate each section? Choose A, B or C.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on the history of postal services.
script: Good morning. Today we're going to look at the history of the postal service, a system so familiar that we rarely think about how revolutionary it once was.

One of the earliest organised systems was created in the Persian Empire, around two and a half thousand years ago. Riders carried messages across the empire, changing horses at stations placed a day's ride apart.
The Romans developed a similar system, but it was only for official messages. Ordinary people had to rely on travellers or private messengers.

A major turning point came in Britain in 1840, when Rowland Hill introduced the Penny Black, the world's first adhesive postage stamp. Before this, letters were usually paid for by the recipient, and the cost depended on the distance travelled and the number of sheets. Hill introduced a cheap, uniform rate, regardless of distance, paid by the sender. The number of letters sent rose dramatically.

In the United States, the Pony Express, launched in 1860, used relays of riders to carry mail across the country in about ten days. It became legendary, but it lasted only eighteen months, because it was replaced by the telegraph.
In the twentieth century, postcodes were introduced in many countries, mainly to help machines sort mail automatically.

Today, the number of letters is falling, but parcel deliveries are increasing rapidly, thanks to online shopping. In some countries, postal services also offer banking, which is especially important in rural areas without bank branches.

passages.title: The Terracotta Army
paragraphs: In March 1974, farmers digging a well near the city of Xi'an in northern China struck fragments of clay. They had stumbled upon one of the greatest archaeological discoveries of the twentieth century: an army of life-sized clay soldiers buried more than two thousand years ago to guard the tomb of China's first emperor.

Qin Shi Huang came to power as king of the state of Qin and, in 221 BC, conquered the rival states to create the first unified Chinese empire. He standardised writing, coins and measurements, and began work on early sections of what would become the Great Wall. He also ordered the construction of a vast tomb complex, on which hundreds of thousands of workers are said to have laboured for decades.

Archaeologists estimate that the pits around the tomb contain about 8,000 soldiers, along with 130 chariots and more than 600 horses. Remarkably, each soldier's face appears to be different, and the figures vary in height, hairstyle and uniform according to their rank. They originally held real weapons, many of which have survived.

Today the soldiers are the colour of the earth, but they were originally brightly painted. When figures are excavated, the paint, which has been preserved by the damp soil, begins to curl and flake within minutes of being exposed to the air. For this reason, archaeologists have been cautious about excavating further until better conservation methods are available.

Studies of the figures suggest that they were produced in a kind of assembly line, with standard body parts made in moulds and then assembled and finished by hand. Many figures carry inscriptions with the names of the workers or workshops that made them, which may have been a form of quality control.

The emperor's tomb itself has never been opened. The ancient historian Sima Qian, writing about a century after the emperor's death, described a tomb containing a model of the empire with rivers of flowing mercury. Scientific surveys have found unusually high levels of mercury in the soil above the tomb, suggesting that his account may contain some truth. Chinese authorities have decided not to excavate the tomb until they can be sure that its contents will not be damaged.

items.q: It was found near the city of ____.

passages.title: The Science of Fermentation
paragraphs: Fermentation is the process by which microorganisms such as yeast and bacteria convert sugars into other substances, such as alcohol, acids or gases. It is one of the oldest food technologies. In a cave in present-day Israel, archaeologists have found evidence that people were brewing a kind of beer around 13,000 years ago, long before the development of farming.

For most of history, fermentation's main value was preservation. The acids produced by bacteria make food too acidic for most harmful microbes to survive, allowing vegetables, milk and fish to be stored for months. On his voyages in the eighteenth century, the explorer James Cook took large quantities of sauerkraut, fermented cabbage, which helped protect his sailors from scurvy, a disease caused by a lack of vitamin C.

Fermented foods are central to many cuisines. In Korea, kimchi, made from fermented cabbage, radish and spices, is eaten with almost every meal. The tradition of kimjang, in which families and neighbours gather in late autumn to prepare large quantities of kimchi for the winter, was recognised by UNESCO as part of the world's intangible cultural heritage in 2013.

In recent years, scientists have become interested in the effects of fermented foods on health. In a 2021 study at Stanford University, volunteers who ate a diet high in fermented foods, such as yoghurt, kefir and kimchi, for ten weeks showed an increase in the diversity of their gut bacteria and a decrease in markers of inflammation in their blood. A group who ate a high-fibre diet did not show the same changes over the same period.

Fermentation is not without risks. If it is carried out incorrectly, for example in conditions that are not acidic enough, harmful bacteria can grow. The most dangerous is the bacterium that causes botulism, a rare but potentially fatal illness. Home fermenters are advised to follow tested recipes carefully.

Today, fermentation is enjoying a revival, both in kitchens and in industry. Chefs are experimenting with traditional techniques, and companies are using a process called precision fermentation, in which microorganisms are programmed to produce specific proteins, such as those found in milk or eggs. Supporters believe this could provide animal-free foods with a much smaller environmental footprint.

groups.instr: Reading Passage 2 has six paragraphs, A–F. Which paragraph contains the following information? Choose the correct letter, A–F.

groups.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

items.q: Why does fermentation help to preserve food?
options: Acids stop harmful microbes from surviving.

passages.title: Holidays in Space
paragraphs: In 2001, the American businessman Dennis Tito paid around 20 million dollars to spend a week on the International Space Station, becoming the world's first space tourist. Two decades later, space tourism entered a new phase. In 2021, two companies founded by billionaires began taking paying passengers on short flights to the edge of space, and the actor William Shatner, then 90 years old, became the oldest person to travel there.

Most of these flights are suborbital: the spacecraft rises above the boundary of space, giving passengers a few minutes of weightlessness and a view of the curved Earth against the blackness of space, before returning to the ground. Tickets have been priced at hundreds of thousands of dollars, far beyond the means of most people.

Supporters argue that space tourism will bring wider benefits. As companies compete and technology improves, they say, costs will fall, making space more accessible for science as well as for tourism. Many astronauts have also described the 'overview effect', a profound change in perspective that comes from seeing the Earth from space, with its thin atmosphere and lack of borders. Some hope that, if more people experience this, it will inspire greater care for the planet.

However, there are serious environmental concerns. Rocket launches release soot, known as black carbon, directly into the upper atmosphere. A study published in 2022 suggested that, because this soot remains in the stratosphere for years, its warming effect is far greater than that of soot from aircraft and other sources. With only a small number of launches today, the overall impact is limited, but it could become significant if space tourism grows as some companies hope.

There are also questions of fairness. At a time when billions of people lack basic necessities, some critics see expensive joyrides for the very wealthy as a symbol of inequality, and argue that the resources involved would be better spent on problems on Earth.

In my view, it would be wrong to ban space tourism, which may indeed help to drive down the costs of reaching space. But I do not think it should be allowed to develop without limits. I believe governments should set limits on rocket emissions and require companies to report their environmental impact, before the industry grows large enough to cause real harm.

groups.instr: Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer in Reading Passage 3? Choose YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.

items.q: Dennis Tito was the first person to pay for a trip into space.
Most people can afford a ticket for a space tourism flight.
Soot from rockets may have a greater warming effect than soot from aircraft.
Space tourism will be cheaper than air travel by 2050.

groups.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

items.q: What do passengers experience on a suborbital flight?

a change in perspective from seeing Earth from space.
a medical problem caused by weightlessness.

options: It stays in the upper atmosphere for years.
It falls back to Earth quickly.

task1.text: The line graph below shows the number of people, in thousands, who travelled to work in one city by four different methods between 1990 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
model: The line graph shows how many people in one city travelled to work by car, bus, train and bicycle between 1990 and 2020.

Overall, the car remained the most common way of commuting throughout the period, although its use declined after 2000. The most dramatic change was the rise in cycling, which by 2020 had overtaken the train.
In 1990, 120,000 people drove to work, while 80,000 took the bus. Far fewer used the train, at 30,000, and only 10,000 cycled.

Car use rose to a peak of 140,000 in 2000, before falling to 110,000 by 2020. Bus use declined gradually from 80,000 to 65,000 in 2010, then recovered slightly to 70,000. The number of train commuters grew steadily, reaching 42,000 in 2020. Cycling, meanwhile, increased slowly until 2000 and then rose sharply, doubling between 2000 and 2010 and reaching 45,000 in 2020, which was four and a half times the 1990 figure.

task2.text: In many countries, printed newspapers are being replaced by online news. Is this a positive or negative development? Write at least 250 words.
model: Over the past two decades, the circulation of printed newspapers has fallen sharply in many countries, as people increasingly get their news online. In my view, this shift has some clear benefits, but overall its effects are more negative than positive, particularly for the quality of public information.

There are certainly advantages to online news. It is fast, so readers can follow events as they happen, and it is often free or cheap. Online articles can include videos, maps and links to original sources, and readers can access news from around the world, not just from their own country. Moving away from print also saves paper and reduces the environmental cost of printing and distribution.

However, the decline of newspapers has serious consequences. Traditional newspapers paid for professional journalists, including reporters who spent months investigating corruption or covering local councils and courts. As advertising revenue has moved to large technology companies, many newspapers have cut staff or closed, and some local communities now have no reliable news source at all. Online, readers often encounter news through social media, where accurate reporting competes with rumours, misleading headlines and deliberate misinformation. Algorithms also tend to show people stories that match their existing views, which can make societies more divided.
These problems are not inevitable. News organisations can develop successful digital subscription models, and governments and charities can support local and investigative journalism.

In conclusion, while online news is convenient and accessible, I believe the decline of printed newspapers has, so far, weakened the quality of information available to the public. The challenge is to find new ways to fund reliable journalism in the digital age.

qs: Do you think you spend too much time looking at screens?

speaking.cue:
Describe a time when you changed your opinion about something.
You should say:
- what your original opinion was
- what made you change it
- what your new opinion is
and explain how you felt about changing your mind.
speaking.cueModel: I'd like to talk about how I changed my opinion about artificial intelligence. When I first started studying computer science, I was quite negative about AI. I'd read a lot of articles saying it would take everyone's jobs and spread fake information, and I thought it was mostly hype created by big technology companies. What changed my mind was a project in my third year. Our group had to build a small application that used natural language processing to help farmers in Bangladesh get information about crop diseases in Bangla, by sending a simple text message. Working on it, I realised how useful these tools could be for people who don't have access to experts, especially in rural areas. I also learned how they actually work, which made them seem less mysterious and frightening. My opinion now is more balanced. I still think there are real risks, such as bias and misinformation, and I think they need careful regulation, but I also believe AI can solve real problems if it's designed responsibly. Changing my mind felt a bit uncomfortable at first, because I'd been quite strongly against it, but now I think it shows that I was open to learning, which is something I'm proud of.
